extracted.intended_audience: poets, critics, and educated readers interested in poetic style and composition (early-18th-century/General literary audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging heroic/epic poems and popular ballads, emphasising simplicity, moral purpose, national character, and naturalness of sentiment. Draws comparisons with ancient models (Homer, Virgil) and exemplifies qualities by the old song 'Chevey-Chase'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of Thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential and inherent Perfection of Simplicity of Thought — 'the first pleases all Kinds of Palates, and the latter only such as have formed to themselves a wrong artificial Taste'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity pleases both ordinary and refined readers (example: Homer, Virgil, Milton). Avoid the 'Gothick Manner' or artificial, epigrammatic turns which please only a small, affected taste. Evidence: Molière's practice of reading comedies to his housekeeper to judge success; the old song 'Chevey Chase' delights common people and refined readers alike because of its simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality / Appeal to Human Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Human Nature is the same in all reasonable Creatures; 'whatever falls in with it, will meet with Admirers amongst Readers of all Qualities and Conditions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for images and sentiments that resonate with common human feeling so that works find admirers across classes. The same 'paintings of Nature' that please ordinary readers will appear beautiful to the most refined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Foundation / Didactic Precept
rubrics_metrics.description: An Heroick Poem should be founded upon some important Precept of Morality, adapted to the Constitution of the Country in which the Poet writes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic subjects should embody and teach a civic or moral lesson relevant to the poet's country (examples: Homer's grounding on Greek discord to encourage union; the ballad's closing lines draw a precept to deter noble quarrels). The poem's moral aim is a central evaluative standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrate Persons and Actions that Honour the Country
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroic poetry ought to 'celebrate Persons and Actions which do Honour to their Country.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer heroes and deeds that raise national reputation (Virgil's hero as founder of Rome, Homer's hero as a prince of Greece). Choosing foreign or irrelevant subjects (e.g., Valerius Flaccus or Statius treating the Golden Fleece) invites derision; local / nationally honouring subjects are preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of National Particulars and Local Detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ national particulars and incidents to raise the reputation of the poet's country (e.g., English and Scotch numbers, differential reactions of kings to news).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific local details and contrasts (troops numbers, kings' responses, locale descriptions) enhance patriotic effect and lend credibility. Such particulars can make a poem laudable for its country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majestic/Natural Simplicity in Diction and Numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: The ballad shows 'majestick Simplicity' and 'sonorous' numbers; natural language and majestic simplicity are praised over affected ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overwrought conceits and prefer language that is both simple and sonorous. The 'Apparel' (diction) of an ancient ballad can be more 'gorgeous' in effect than later affected styles; sound and cadence ('numbers') matter for poetic dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Epigrammatical Turns and Artificial Wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Had this old Song been filled with Epigrammatical Turns and Points of Wit, it might perhaps have pleased the wrong Taste ... but it would never have become the Delight of the common People.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from prioritising clever epigrams or fashionable conceits at the expense of natural sentiment and public appeal; such artifices narrow the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: Actions and Sentiments Fitting a Hero
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sentiments and Actions of a hero should be 'every Way suitable to an Hero' — e.g., single combat, generosity, exhorting men even in dying, and noble lamentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict heroic figures through fitting behavior (bravery, honour, pity, magnanimity). Concrete examples: Earl Douglas offering single combat, exhorting his men on his death, Piercy's generous lament and the gesture of 'Taking the dead Man by the Hand' which echoes noble classical models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not Let Simple Style Prejudice the Reader Against Greatness of Thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution: 'the Simplicity of the Stile, which one may well pardon in so old a Poet, [should not] prejudice him against the Greatness of the Thought.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers and critics should distinguish between plain diction and weakness of conception; simple phrasing can contain lofty thought. Writers may use plain style without sacrificing intellectual or emotional depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Consequences / Consideration of Posterity
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic perspective can and should consider future consequences of present actions ('The Child may rue that was unborn ...'), anticipating how present quarrels will affect posterity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In heroic narrative, gestures that indicate concern for posterity or long-term effects enrich moral weight (example stanza cited as similar to Horace's thought about posterity hearing ancestral wars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek Resonance with Classical Models without Imitation-for-its-own-sake
rubrics_metrics.description: The ballad's passages 'are written in the Spirit of Virgil' — similarity to ancient poets arises from shared 'kind of Poetical Genius' and 'copyings after Nature', not mere imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for the qualities that make classical poetry powerful (natural grandeur, majesty, moral weight) rather than mechanically borrowing classical phrases or incidents. Use classical parallels as confirmation of natural poetic genius, not as formulaic templates.
